906.tone: Loving 1966 analyses Awa as a syllable-tone language: 'Awa tonemes include high, falling, rising, and low'; 'Only one toneme occurs with any' syllable; minimal pairs on monosyllables (na 'breast'/'taro'/'house'); 23 of 64 patterns attested on trisyllables; text frequencies low 68%, high 22.8%, falling 5.4%, rising 3.8%. The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur in the paper, nor in the Lovings' 1975 Awa Dictionary (PL C-30), whose grammar sketch says only 'Tone is not indicated as this changes depending on the stems with which these affixes occur.'

909.dq: A word with clitics, relevant to accentuation, will be called an accent unit. This is equivalent with the phonological word. ... The accent unit, or phonological word, is a complex of words and clitics, that share a single accent.
909.dloc: sect. 2.4 Syllable structure (pp. 42-43: |v| = long vowel; heavy = |-vc|, |-əcc|, |-vcc|); sect. 2.5-2.5.2.2 Accent (pp. 43-45); sect. 1.3 Notes on terminology of word structure (p. 7); sect. 1.3.1 The accent unit (p. 8); sect. 4.3.3.13 (antepenult token ásənsər)
909.heavy: Sect. 2.4: '|v| stands for any long vowel (a, i, u, e, o) and |ə| stands for the short vowel ə.... Syllables that end in |-vc|, |-əcc| and |-vcc| are all considered heavy. All other syllables are considered light.' I.e. heavy = full ('long') vowel + coda C(C), or schwa + CC; open |cv|, |cə| and closed |cəc| are light. Only the weight of the FINAL syllable of the accent unit matters for default accent (final if heavy, else penult).
909.prule: Default accent on the accent unit (phonological word = word + clitics): final syllable if the unit ends in a heavy syllable (|-vc(c)#| or |-əcc#|; note |-əc#| is light), otherwise penultimate. Accent moves rightward when plural suffixes or possessive/deictic clitics are added.

910.tone: Both primaries agree Awngi is a tone language (Hetzron 1976: Mid/High/Low/Falling, the last two word-final only; Joswig 2010: H/L plus word-final falling = H+L, Hetzron's extra-low is a positional variant). The disagreement is only about a coexisting weak penultimate intensity stress: Hetzron asserts it (1969, 1976, 1978, 1997), Joswig (later phonology-focused fieldwork) finds no evidence. Joswig p.18 notes the [ʊ]~[uː] alternation by tone as 'a indicator that the prosodic system of the Awngi language is actually based on a pitch-accent system' but in 4.2 concludes tone cannot be reduced to a stress feature.

tn.quote: Awngi has two distinctive tone levels, high and low. On word-final syllables these two tones can combine to create a falling tone. ... [p.20] There are three tones that can apply to a single syllable: high, low and falling. The falling tone appears only on the last syllable of a word, although in contrast to the other two. ... [p.21] The falling tone seems to be a sequence of high and low. ... [fn.32, p.22] I found no evidence in the varieties of Awngi which I have studied of the “weak stress of intensity” attested by Hetzron (1978:123) on the penultimate syllable.

tn.note: Two level tones (H, L); word-final falling = H+L sequence; Hetzron's mid/extra-low reanalysed as low variants; floating H/L stem tones; roots all-L, all-H or L..H; author finds no penultimate stress.

910.cfw: Hetzron (1969, 1976, 1997) describes a penultimate demarcative stress operating alongside tone, Worku Gela (1986) instead puts stress on the first syllable (final in adjectives, adverbs and imperatives), and Joswig (2010), the fullest phonology of the language, treats Awngi as a two-level tone language and could not confirm any independent stress, so first-hand descriptions disagree on whether Awngi has word stress at all and, if it does, where it falls. The Kunfäl (Kulazngi) dialect is described separately below from its own source, with a three-level tone inventory.

variants.name: Kunfäl (Kulazngi / Kulisi Agaw), dialect of Awngi
variants.prule: No word-stress rule. Kulazngi (Kunfäl) is described as a lexical and grammatical tone language: every syllable of a word bears one of three level tones (H, M, L) or a falling HL contour; tone distinguishes lexemes (múrí H.H 'snake' vs mùrí L.H 'village') and grammatical forms. The grammar never states where stress falls and uses 'stress' only of Kemanteney.
variants.quote: By all definitions above, Kulazngi is a tone language, or it is not a mere pitch-accent language, because every syllable in a word bears low, mid, or high tone having a lexical as well as a grammatical function. A significant number of lexical items of the same word class show meaning variation due to pitch variation only. Pitch also plays a role to express grammatical distinction. ... In Kulazngi, the tone carried in a syllable may be an essential feature in determining the meaning or the grammatical feature of the word. For example, ... bér (H) 'gate', múrí (H.H) 'snake', and mùrí (L.H) 'village'. Hence, Kulazngi is a tone language with the above three tone levels (high, low, mid) plus a falling tone both at a lexical and a morphological level [p. 44] ... Among the Agaw languages, Bilin and Awngi are reported to be tone languages while Kemanteney has only stress (Hetzron, 1976: 2). ... the present study reveals that every syllable of Kulazngi words carries a relative pitch accent among which some are contrastive, which distinguish between various lexical and grammatical forms, which is a feature that places a language at tonal position. ... In this study, Kulazngi has three level (high, low, mid) and one contour (HL) tones. Each level tone can appear with monosyllabic and disyllabic words. While high and low tones have no positional restriction, mid tone never occurs word initially in polysyllabic words; it does not occur sequentially (as M.M) either. [p. 45]

High tone and Low tone may be said to be basic in Efutu as they may occur independently in words. Unlike High and Low tone, Downstep-high and Falling appear to be secondary; they usually do not occur independently.

913.dq: speakers of the language tend to reject such long forms when written as a single word, and instead divide them up into their individual roots, which each retain stress in complex forms and so constitute distinct phonological words: kilolopâ päko manato. (p. 5); 'As a main rule, stress in Äiwoo falls on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable of a word' (p. 2)
913.dloc: Introduction 'The Äiwoo language', §1.1 Spelling, p. 2 (silent vowels + stress main rule); p. 5 (roots as distinct phonological words)
913.prule: Main rule: stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. Perturbation 1 (segmental, vowel height): high vowels i/u devoice or drop when unstressed, and stress is shifted away from a high vowel onto a preceding syllable when one is available (nubo [ˈnuᵐbo] vs inubo [ˈinᵐbo], i.e. antepenult by underlying syllable count), subject to a no-consecutive-deletion constraint (ngâgumu [ŋɑˈᵑgumʷ]). Perturbation 2 (morphological/domain): roots retain their own stress in complex forms and constitute distinct phonological words; pre-stress lengthened vowels (historical roots) take secondary stress.
913.srule: Næss 2017: 2: a vowel lengthened in pre-stress position typically carries secondary stress (paveli ~ paaveli 'garden'), which Næss attributes to the lengthened syllable being a historical root; no general rhythmic rule in that source. Fuller rule (Næss in prep., reported by Viken 2024: 16-17): in a monomorphemic word, secondary stress on the leftmost mora of each bimoraic foot preceding the final (main-stressed) foot, feet built right-to-left over morae (a single left-over mora is unstressed: tememe (te)(ˈme.me)).
913.quote: No special indication is made of the so-called ‘silent vowels’. This term refers to the fact that, in some positions, the high vowels [i] and [u] are pronounced voicelessly (i.e. like a whisper) or dropped altogether. Simplifying somewhat, the rule is that these vowels are dropped in unstressed position (e.g. laki [ˈlakh] ‘be small’, nenu [ˈnenʷ] ‘coconut’), and that stress is shifted away from these vowels if there is a preceding syllable which can take stress (nubo [ˈnuᵐbo] ‘die’, but inubo [ˈinᵐbo] ‘he/she died’). It is not possible to drop vowels in consecutive syllables ... ngâgu [ˈŋɑᵑgʷ…
913.loc: Introduction 'The Äiwoo language', §1.1 Spelling, p. 2 (silent vowels + stress main rule); p. 5 (roots as distinct phonological words)
913.idn: Äiwoo ('Reefs', 'Ayiwo') as spoken in the Main Reef Islands, Temotu Province, Solomon Islands; the dictionary does not single out one dialect (two recognised dialect areas, Fenua Loa + northern Lomlom vs coastal Lomlom + Gawâ; 'My own knowledge of the language is not sufficient to identify dialectal differences'…
913.exq_: As a main rule, stress in Äiwoo falls on the penultimate (next-to-last) syllable of a word, but it is also to some extent tied to morphological structure, in that roots typically retain their individual stress in complex forms.

915.dq: In nouns, stress accent falls on the initial syllable and in the verb category stress accent falls on the final syllable.
915.dloc: sec. 4.3.2 'Stress', thesis p. 196; summary restated in ch. 'Conclusion'; tone in sec. 4.3.3 pp. 196-197
915.prule: Marginal word stress, stated only for disyllables and conditioned on word class: nouns carry initial-syllable stress, verbs carry final-syllable stress (ˈbəlla 'evil spirit' vs bəˈlla 'call'). No rule given for longer words; no weight condition stated. Otherwise stress is described as an emphasis device (length + pitch). Tone (three tones, Punjabi-type) is the prominent suprasegmental.
915.quote: 4.3.2 Stress. The stress is not an important feature of Bagri, yet, it seems that its existence and phonemic status cannot be ruled out. morph.rootq: General rule is stated over the WORD, not the root (Fraser 1891 p.74): 'The accent is generally on the penultimate vowel, and runs on into the following consonant. The final vowel, in most cases, is very lightly touched. An exception to the general accent is when a word ends in a diphthong. In such cases the diphthongs are usually accented. When a word ends in io or iu the accent is generally on the vowel before them.' Morphology enters only indirectly, via the tense prefix: p.85 'Verbs beginning with ma, me, mi, mo, mu, and accented on the first vowel, do not undergo any change in the future tense. (Mudri is an exception.)'; p.86 'In verbs beginning with mi, or its remnant m, the mi is…
morph.elicq: No statement of the evidential basis. Fraser (resident missionary on Epi) simply asserts: 'The accent is generally on the penultimate vowel, and runs on into the following consonant. The final vowel, in most cases, is very lightly touched.' (1891 p.74). Ray 1926 worked second-hand from Fraser's grammar and the Gospel translations ('Mr Fraser remarks that ...', §2; 'Mr Fraser has the example ... I find no examples in the translations', §48) and adds no accent observations of his own beyond §27.
morph.stmt: Neither sketch gives a one-line typological profile; assembled from their statements, Baki is weakly affixing and split by word class: the verb is inflected at its LEFT edge — obligatory preposed short subject pronouns ('A verb cannot be used without these', Fraser p.78; 'The Baki verb is conjugated by means of the short subjective pronouns', Ray §31) and a nonfuture prefix mi-/m- with initial-consonant mutation ('formed in a majority of verbs by prefixing mi or its abbreviation m to the simple WB', Ray §31), plus preverbal mbi and the univerbated causative verb la-; object pronouns are 'shortened objective pronouns, or verbal suffixes... so, o, lo' after the verb (Fraser p.79), and…

920.dq: Word stress in Balangao is phonemic, occurring on the ultimate or penultimate syllable of a full grammatical word, with or without affixes. ... [p. 32] Stress, however, is often difficult to discern. The reasons: 1) the added mora of length occurs only on non-final CV syllables and no others, 2) intensity may be obscured when the stressed syllable occurs in the margins of a phonological stress gr…
920.dloc: Sec. 1.5 'Stress', pp. 31-32; Sec. 1.51-1.52 pp. 32-34; Sec. 1.61 'Stress shift', p. 35; Sec. 1.1 'Word', p. 19
920.heavy: Only fused long vowels (CVV, two moras from historical vowel fusion) are said to attract/retain stress: 'Stress always occurs on these fused vowels, resisting the normal morphophonemic change of stress upon suffixation'. Otherwise placement within the window is lexical, not weight-computed; stressed non-final CV syllables gain a mora of length (length is a correlate of stress, not its conditioner).
920.prule: Phonemic (contrastive) word stress restricted to the final two syllables (ultimate or penultimate) of a full word; minimal pairs 'hawang/ha'wang, 'qale/qa'le. Secondary stress on every second syllable counting back from the main stress (clitics excluded).
920.srule: Rhythmic secondary stress (Sec. 1.5, p. 31): 'A secondary stress occurs on every second syllable counting back from the main stress: pa"gingi'nahal 'sandy place', "bale'ngawngaw 'circle', qo"menpa"bale'ngawngaw 'cause it to be circled''; clitics carry their own stress but 'Clitics do not set up secondary stress.' The primary itself shifts under suffixation (Sec. 1.61 'Stress shift', p. 35, a morphophonemic rule, not a secondary-stress rule): 'When a root is suffixed, the stress of that root is shifted either one or two syllables to the right toward the suffix. If the final two syllables are of the pattern 'CVCV, the stress shifts two syllables and occurs on the suffix... If the final syllables of a root are of any pattern other than 'CVCV, the stress shifts only one syllable... When vowels fuse to form CVVC syllable pattern, stress always occurs on the syllable and does not shift'.
920.quote: Word stress in Balangao is phonemic, occurring on the ultimate or penultimate syllable of a full grammatical word, with or without affixes. All full words (see Sec. 1.1) must have stress. 922.prule: Conservative Romani ('grammatical') stress: inherited nouns/adjectives stress the final syllable in Nom.Sg. and Nom.Pl. (i.e. the last syllable of the inherited stem + Layer-I inflection); in oblique cases stress sits on the oblique marker (-és-, -á-, -én-) while the following Layer-II case suffixes stay unstressed (čhavéske); vocative endings partly stressed (-éja, -íje) and partly unstressed (phrál-a); borrowed nouns stress the syllable before the final thematic vowel (penult), more rarely one further back, but again the oblique marker in oblique cases; finite verbs stress the person ending (-áv-, -és-, -él-; pret. -óm-, -án-), d-final verbs the syllable before it; loan verbs likewise. Position is thus set by morpheme identity and etymological layer (inherited vs. borrowed), not by syllable count or weight. Balkan-branch specifics: Arli mostly keeps this archaic state but allows optional retraction to the antepenult (Macedonian influence: šukaripé ~ šukáripe); Bugurdži shows it 'very poorly', with word accent fluctuating with sentence rhythm, polysyllabic verbs often antepenult, loan verbs stress -íz-; Prizren has generalised penult stress in Nom./Obl. of nouns, adjectives, pronouns and in the preterite (few exceptions, among them Turkisms), but keeps stress on the oblique morpheme in other cases.

evidence_works.detail: Adds the standard formulation of Romani grammatical stress that the entry's coding (kind = morphological, from Boretzky & Igla 1994 sec. 1.4) rests on: 'Early Romani had word-level grammatical stress, which is preserved in contemporary Romani in what Boretzky and Igla (1993) call ‘conservative’ stress patterns. In the pre-European (‘thematic’) component, stress is on the final position of lexical roots, in the absence of grammatical affixes, or on older grammatical affixes: sastó ‘healthy’' (pp. 62-63) and 'conservative stress in the pre-European (thematic) component falls on Layer I inflectional endings in nominal and nominalised categories' (p. 63). For the Balkan varieties the entry treats it names the contact trigger and the variability the entry's dq quote records: 'The second centre is in the Balkans. Here the trigger is likely to be in the complex patterns of Albanian, which often result in penultimate stress. The affected dialects include varieties of Bugurdži, Arli, and others. In both groups, the process still appears to be ongoing and stress is subject to variation. Consistent shifts are reported for the Terzi Mahale dialect of Prizren (penultimate)' (p. 64).

924.heavy: Closed (CVC) final syllable 'usually carries primary stress' in trisyllables; but CV.CVC disyllabic nouns/adjectives are predominantly penult-stressed, so closure is a hedged tendency, not a rule. 'Length is not a factor in stress assignment'.
924.dflt: penultimate in disyllables (CV.CV, CV.VC exceptionless); final primary + antepenult secondary in trisyllables
924.prule: One primary stress per word, penultimate or final. Disyllables CV.CV / CV.VC: penultimate without exception. CV.CVC, CVC.CVC, CVC.CV: nouns/adjectives predominantly penultimate (trochaic), verbs and other word classes vary between penult and final. Trisyllables: tend to final primary + antepenultimate secondary, 'in particular a closed final syllable usually carries primary stress'. Quadrisyllables: penultimate or final. Secondary stress never adjacent to primary. Author suggests an underlying trochaic system disturbed by historical final-vowel/consonant loss; length plays no role.
924.srule: Words of three or more syllables mostly carry one secondary stress, never adjacent to the primary: trisyllables with final primary have it on the antepenultimate (initial) syllable [ˌkɐ.lɐ.'si], those with initial primary on the final ['nɐ.lu.ˌɐj]; quadrisyllables (incl. all 3-4-syllable -ek forms) have it on the first syllable [ˌku.ru.'ru.pɐ], [ˌte.re.pe.'lɛk]; inherently reduplicated trisyllabic nouns with initial primary show no clear secondary ['kul.ku.lu]. No words over four syllables.
924.quote: In each word, there is one syllable that receives primary stress. tn.quote: Prosody refers to suprasegmental features of speech, as opposed to segmental phonology. Relevant features for Paluai include stress and intonation. 2.3.1 Stress In words that contain more than one syllable, there are some syllables that are more prominent than others. This prominence is due to more acoustic energy, mainly loudness and pitch, and can be conveniently called ‘stress’. Length is not a factor in stress assignment: Paluai does not have contrastive vowel length and stressed vowels do not appear to be longer than unstressed vowels.
tn.cite: Schokkin, Gerda Hendrike. 2014. A grammar of Paluai: the language of Baluan Island, Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, James Cook University, Cairns. 548 pp. doi:10.25903/tpm1-j309.
tn.note: Prosody analysed as word stress plus sentence intonation only; pitch is a correlate of stress and of intonation (one main pitch rise per sentence); no lexical tone is described.

924.cfw: The only description of Paluai stress is Schokkin's reference grammar (2014 thesis, published 2020), which states that each word has one primary stress on the penult or the final syllable, largely predictable from syllable shape and word class but with many lexical exceptions, and no other source has described the language.

925.prule: No stress. Two level tones (H, L); the tonal domain usually coincides with the word: an initial tonally dominant syllable with lexical tone plus recessive syllables whose tones are rule-assigned; floating-L article; downdrift/downstep. Disyllabic 'featural' feet differ only in first-vowel length ('heavy' CV:CV vs 'light' CVCV); V1 reduction/elision in light feet (fúlá ~ flá) is phonetic and phonotactically conditioned; V2 is long word-finally ('foot isochrony'). Vydrin 2020 explicitly withdraws his 2014 'foot stress' (iambic 2nd-syllable prominence) analysis: 'there is no need to postulate the existence of stress'.
925.srule: None: the source denies word stress altogether -- 'there is no need to postulate the existence of stress'; Bambara is 'a language with a featural foot and no stress' (no secondary or rhythmic stress is described; heavy/light feet are durational, not stress feet).

925.idn: Bambara (also Bamana, Bamanankan), Manding < Western Mande; the experimental data are from two native speakers of the village of Dugukunna near Segu; dictionary data from Bailleul 2007 and Dumestre 2011 (Vydrin 2014 fn.7 adds that his data are 'standard Bamana', formed on the basis of the Bamako dialect); data…
925.tone: Two level tones, high and low (low arguably the marked one, Creissels 2009); word-initial syllable tonally dominant, tone spreads right over recessive syllables to the end of the wordform or the next dominant syllable; floating-L referential article; downdrift and downstep. On stress/accent: Vydrin 2014 posited a foot-level 'stress' in iambic feet that was neither obligatory nor culminative at word level and did not interact with tone; Vydrin 2020 (instrumental study, same author) retracts this: foot types reduce to first-vowel length, V1 elision is phonetic, and Bambara is 'a language with a featural foot and no stress'. Tonal dominance is stated to be non-isomorphic with foot headedness. Green 2010/2015 (uniformly trochaic feet, L-to-R) and Leben 2002/2003 (tonal feet) analyse the foot differently but likewise as a tonal/segmental domain, not a stress position.

Rules hedged as 'qui semblent être très générales'. A few nouns are said to lack the accent altogether, and presence vs absence of accent distinguishes meaning (bánga/banga, góngou/gongou, kókora/kokora, n'gánga/n'ganga, d'édé/dédé) — 'de cas peu fréquent'.

tn.translation: ACCENT. The Banda language is sung, that is, each syllable has its own pitch and is pronounced on a higher or lower tone than its neighbour. Three principal tones are distinguished: the high tone, in n6 [scan; nó?], di, kä 'all'; the mid tone, in enji 'they'; the low tone, in mbwänga 'palaver'. ... Besides the pitch accent, there exists in Banda an accent of intensity which affects certain syllables of words, so that the unaccented syllables shorten and tend to disappear

928.prule: Main accent on the stem-initial syllable: for nouns, the first syllable of the word once the class ('alliterative') prefix is stripped; for verbs, the first syllable of the root. 928.srule: Secondary accent on each alternate syllable both before and after the main (stem-initial) accent: 'Each alternate syllable, whether before or after this main accented one, receives a secondary accent.'

morph.stmt: Whitehead describes Bobangi words as a mono- or disyllabic base flanked by 'formative syllables' on both sides — "Those which are placed before the stem are called formative prefixes, or preformatives. 930.prule: Ramirez 2001 states an explicit rule: the (pitch) accent never falls on the final syllable and always falls on the syllable immediately preceding the last metrical syllable of the phonological word, i.e. generally the penult; suffixes are lexically metrical or extrametrical (listed in the dictionary), and extrametrical suffixes are invisible to the count, so the accent can surface on the antepenult or earlier. (Souza 2012, a different work, reports only the penult-dominant distribution.)
930.srule: Not mentioned in Souza 2012 (sec. 4.6.2 'Acento e duração', pp. 185-191; his 'segundo acento' is the H vs LH contour inside the stressed heavy syllable, a tone fact). Ramirez 2001 (sec. 2.1.5, pp. 88-96) treats the primary accent only ('Limitaremo-nos... ao acento primário'; one and only one prominent syllable per phonological word) and gives no secondary placement. tn.quote: O Baníwa-Currípaco possuí duas rnelodías tonais nas V longas mas só uma nas V breves: - cada palavra fonológica possui só uma sílaba fonologicamente tôníca, - se a sílaba tôníca é do tipo [(C)(h)VJ (isto é com V breve), a melodia acentual que cai nela só pode ser um tom alto … se a sílaba tôn ica é do tipo [(C)(h) V: 1 (isto é com V longa), a melodia acentual que cai nela pode ser de dois tipos em oposição: um tom de registro alto … ou um tom de contorno ascendente … Isso nos permite interpretar, em subjacente, o Baniwa-Curripaco como urna língua de« pitch- accent »e não como uma língua tonal.
tn.translation: Baniwa-Curripaco has two tonal melodies on long vowels but only one on short vowels: - each phonological word has only one phonologically tonic syllable, - if the tonic syllable is of the type [(C)(h)V] (i.e. with short V), the accentual melody that falls on it can only be a high tone ... if the tonic syllable is of the type [(C)(h)V:] (i.e. with long V), the accentual melody that falls on it can be of two types in opposition: a high register tone ... or a rising contour tone ... This allows us to interpret Baniwa-Curripaco, underlyingly, as a 'pitch-accent' language and not as a tonal language.
tn.cite: Ramirez, Henri. 2001. Línguas Arawak da Amazônia Setentrional: Comparação e Descrição. Manaus: EDUA (Editora da Universidade do Amazonas).
tn.note: Pitch accent, one per word, never word-final; accented short vowels carry high tone, accented long vowels/diphthongs contrast high (V́V) vs rising (VV́), i.e. accent on 1st vs 2nd mora; not tonal.

930.cfw: Ramirez's 2001 reference grammar and dictionary give a near-exceptionless rule placing the pitch accent on the syllable before the last metrical syllable (never on the final syllable, with a dictionary-listed set of extrametrical suffixes that pushes surface accent to the antepenult or earlier), Taylor 1991 independently treats the penult as the unmarked position, and Souza 2012, the shorter master's thesis behind the 'variable' coding, reports the same penult-dominant surface spread without proposing a rule, so the reading is well supported even though only one description states the rule in full.

ev.text: Word stress is unpredictable and therefore phonemic. Stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable: kayu wood, baley house, makapala? thick. In a large number of words it falls on the final syllable, this being synchronically unpredictable: maheme full, mabaha? heavy, lumampa[ng] to walk. In other words stress falls on the third-last syllable: likudu? back, dakele? many. Stress contrast is shown by the following pairs: saha[ng] tree sp. and saha[ng] ant, mamuku (stem buku) to kneel and mamuku (stem puku) to bend, pahigi well and pahigi knife. In the present work stress in Ban is indicated wherever it does not fall on the penultimate syllable of the word.

The pitch accent nucleus is indicated by an apostrophe at the beginning of the syllable. ... Lexical stress is also important in Bantik. ... In Bantik, a word can exhibit different pitch patterns depending on the environment. ... the sentential intonation pattern overwrites the lexical pitch pattern ... In summary, a final IU in a sentence always shows a falling pitch, even if the last syllable of the IU is stressed and has a high pitch.

tn.note: One lexical accent per word, free among the last three syllables, realised as high pitch; Utsumi calls it both 'phonemic pitch accent' and 'lexical phonemic stress'; Sneddon 1984 says stress.
